newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece to issue 12-mth T-bills at 9.6 pct Jun 2.
newsitem.headline: Greece to issue 12-mth T-bills at 9.6 pct Jun 2.

text.p: Greece will issue 12-month T-bills at 9.60 percent, down 10 basis points, on June 2 and reopen bids for three-, five- and 10-year fixed coupon bonds on June 19, Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis told reporters.

"We will issue dematerialised 12-month T-bills at 9.60 percent on June 2," Christodoulakis told reporters. "We will also reopen bids for three-, five- and seven-year fixed coupon bonds on June 19 when we will auction 10-year fixed coupon bonds."
Greece auctioned three-year, 9.8 percent fixed coupon bonds, five-year, 9.2 percent coupon bonds and seven-year, 8.9 percent coupon bonds on March 19.

"The finance ministry will set the coupon for the 10-year fixed coupon bond and announce amounts for the three-, five-, seven- and 10-year fixed coupon bonds in the near future," said Christodoulakis.
The treasury raised 38 billion drachmas from the sale of 4.0 percent, five-year CPI-indexed bonds and 32 billion drachmas from the 4.0 percent, 10-year CPI-indexed bonds on May 19, the minister said.
"The domestic borrowing programme is going smoothly," said Christodoulakis. "I might be in a position to make public the public borrowing schedule for 1998 next week."

Asked to comment on the IMF draft report on the Greek economy that was made public on Wednesday, the minister said the government was determined to stick to Greece's EU convergence plan and structural reforms had been already initiated.
The IMF praised Greece's economic progress in 1996 but said macroeconomic policy should get tighter and structural reforms must be accelerated to meet 1997 targets set out in its EU convergence plan.

"The finance ministry has asked all ministries and subsidised entities to submit their 1998 budgets by June 23 so that there is plenty of time to prepare the 1998 budget," said Christodoulakis. "This takes place for the first time in Greece."
The goal is to evaluate their performance and proceed with a more rational allocation of resources, he added. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
